holding_summary: In a burglary-insurance dispute over a stolen ring, the court held that clear proof excluding every other cause of loss suffices as proof of theft, and that the presence of paying boarders/lodgers in plaintiff's home did not breach a policy warranty limiting occupancy to "the assured and family alone," because the policy itself contemplated boarders and lodgers and the word "family" includes them.

quotes.text: the term assured as used in this policy shall be construed to mean the individual named or any relative or other member of the household of suph individual actually residing in the premises who does not pay board or rent, excepting domestic servants and employees.

But the policy contains no prohibition against the taking of boarders and lodgers; on the contrary it clearly permits it, since it provides ex industria against liability for losses suffered by any such boarder or lodger, when a member of the household, to-wit:

the word "family” in the aforementioned warranty is therein used in its proper etymological as well as legal sense, to-wit, as compromising all who live in one household under one head even boarders and lodgers.

notes: Ordinary residential lease repair-liability case; the 'family member' issue concerns a resident mother-in-law, not compensated boarding/lodging.

holding_summary: A long-term paying resident of a YMCA sued for theft from his room; the court held the YMCA was a charitable institution, not a lodging house, hotel, or innkeeper making a business of lodging travelers, and therefore not liable under innkeeper doctrine, distinguishing its member-residency arrangement from commercial lodging.

quotes.text: This corporation is created by an act of the Legislature of 1873. It is commonly known as a charitable institution and not as a hotel or rooming house, it is so only incidentally, and during ths late military activities it served thousands of soliders, the rentals, if any were for malntainence and not for profit.
